t: Minimum Number of Operations to Make Word K-Periodic
o: The string is split into n/k consecutive blocks of length k. One operation copies any block over another, so the cheapest way to make all blocks identical is to pick the block content that already occurs most often and overwrite every other block with it. Each overwritten block costs exactly one operation, so the answer is (number of blocks) minus (count of the most frequent block). For "leetcodeleet" with k=4 there are 3 blocks: leet, code, leet — the majority appears twice, so 3-2=1. For "leetcoleet" with k=2 there are 5 blocks: le, et, co, le, et — the max frequency is 2, so 5-2=3. Since k divides n and n can be up to 1e5, we just need an O(n) counting pass; no search or DP is needed.
k: A word is k-periodic exactly when every length-k block starting at a multiple of k is identical.
One operation can rewrite one whole block to match any other block, so each non-majority block needs exactly one operation.
Answer = (n/k) - max frequency of any block among the n/k blocks.
Hashing each block substring into a frequency map gives an O(n) solution.

a.i: For every pair of blocks, count how many blocks equal a given block and take the maximum. This directly implements 'majority block' but recompares substrings repeatedly, costing O(n^2 / k * k) = O(n^2 / k) time in the worst case — too slow for large inputs but conceptually simple.
s: Split indices 0, k, 2k, ... as block starts.
For each block i, count blocks j whose substring equals block i.
a.t: O(n^2 / k) — for each of the m = n/k blocks we compare against all m blocks, each comparison O(k).
a.sp: O(n) — storing or slicing all block substrings.

a.n: Approach 2: Hash map counting of blocks (optimal)
a.i: Instead of comparing pairs, insert every block into a hash map keyed by its substring and keep frequencies. The most frequent block is the one we keep; everything else needs one copy operation. This is a single linear pass over the string.
s: Initialize an empty hash map from block string to count.
a.t: O(n) — each character belongs to exactly one block; hashing each block costs O(k), summed over all blocks this is O(n) expected.
a.sp: O(n) — up to n/k distinct block keys of length k stored in the hash map.

w: In an interview, go straight to the hash-map approach after stating the key reduction: answer = number of blocks minus the maximum block frequency. Common pitfalls: forgetting that k always divides n (so no partial blocks exist), off-by-one errors at block boundaries (use range(0, n, k)), and assuming operations must copy adjacent blocks — any pair of multiples of k works, which is why one op per fixed block suffices. Edge cases: k = n (answer is 0 since there is a single block), and a word that is already k-periodic (max frequency equals block count, answer 0). A likely follow-up: what if k did not divide n, or if you wanted the lexicographically smallest resulting periodic string — the latter would require choosing among tied majority blocks.
